2026-11-10.title: A new moon: prepare the ground
2026-11-10.caption:
Tonight, a new moon opens the season of preparation.

Jumada al-Akhirah is expected to begin tomorrow, in shaa Allah. After it comes Rajab, the month of planting, then Sha'ban, the month of watering, and then Ramadan, the harvest, in shaa Allah. Before any seed goes in, a farmer clears the ground.

This week, look honestly at what fills your evenings. Choose one habit to reduce gently, then give the time it frees to one small act for Allah: a few minutes of dhikr, one page of Qur'an, a call to someone you love. Nothing dramatic. Just ground made ready.

The early scholars described this season beautifully: "Rajab is the month of planting, Sha'ban the month of watering, and Ramadan the month of harvest" (Abu Bakr al-Balkhi, quoted by Ibn Rajab).

Today's journal prompt: Which ordinary task could become worship today with one intention?

2026-11-12.title: Good that keeps growing
2026-11-12.caption:
Some good keeps growing long after we have gone.

The Prophet ﷺ told us that when a person dies, their deeds end except for three: ongoing charity, knowledge that benefits others, and a righteous child who makes du'a for them (Sahih Muslim).

This week, choose one seed that fits your life. It could be a small monthly gift to a water well or a mosque, something you know well and could teach a sister, or a habit of du'a you share with your children. Make it real with one practical step, then make a sincere niyyah and ask Allah to accept it. What grows from it is in His hands.

Planted now, it will already be growing when Ramadan arrives.

2026-11-13.title: The middle path
2026-11-13.caption:
A plan you can keep on hard days is a good plan.

It is Jumu'ah, a good day to look at your Ramadan hopes with honest, gentle eyes.

The Prophet ﷺ told us that the religion is ease, and that whoever overburdens himself in it will be overcome (Bukhari). This is the middle path: steady worship, kept with sincerity, sized to the life Allah has given you.

Try this. Write down one act of worship you would love to keep in Ramadan. Then decide its floor: the smallest amount you will do even on a day of fever, deadlines or a teething baby. Practise that floor every day for a week. When it feels steady, add one small step.

And since it is Friday, read Surah al-Kahf and send salawat on the Prophet ﷺ.

2026-11-14.title: Water
2026-11-14.caption:
Your suhoor glass of water starts today.

In Ramadan, you will go long hours without a sip. The body adjusts more gently when it already knows a steady rhythm of water.

Here is a simple habit to begin this week: one glass after each salah. Five prayers, five glasses, no app needed. Drink in three breaths, as the Prophet ﷺ did (Muslim), begin with Bismillah, and close with Alhamdulillah. Allah tells us He made every living thing from water (21:30), so each glass is a small sign to reflect on.

Water is also a beautiful form of sadaqa. If you have a little to give this week, think of a well, a water cooler at your masjid, or a cold bottle handed to a worker in the heat.

2026-11-15.title: Share your table
2026-11-15.caption:
Who could eat at your table this week?

In a few months, many of us will host iftars. A heart that opens its door easily in Ramadan has usually been trained in ordinary weeks.

The Prophet ﷺ was asked which deed in Islam is best, and he answered: feed people, and greet those you know and those you do not (Bukhari, Muslim). He also told us that whoever gives a fasting person iftar has a reward like theirs (Tirmidhi).

This week, cook a little more of one dish and send a plate next door. Or invite one person who often eats alone. Keep the food simple and the welcome warm. Make your niyyah before you serve, and leave the rest with Allah.

2026-11-16.title: Move your body
2026-11-16.caption:
Tarawih begins with your legs, long before the first night.

In Ramadan, you will stand for longer prayers, wake earlier, and still carry your work and your family. A body that moves a little every day carries all of this with more ease.

The Prophet ﷺ said the strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak one, and in both there is good (Muslim). Strength here includes faith and resolve, and a healthy body helps you live both.

This week, choose ten minutes: a walk after Asr with dhikr, a stretch after Fajr, or two sunnah rak'ahs where you stand a little longer. Make the niyyah that this strength is for worship. On days you cannot do much, a slow walk around the house counts too.

2026-11-17.title: Be gentle with yourself
2026-11-17.caption:
Would you speak to a friend the way you speak to yourself?

Ramadan preparation can start with a long list and a harsh inner voice: pray more, read more, be better. The list is sincere. The voice can be gentler.

The Prophet ﷺ taught that Allah is Gentle and loves gentleness in all matters (Bukhari, Muslim). All matters includes the way you plan, and the way you speak to yourself when a plan slips.

This week, write one honest sentence about your season of life: the broken nights, the deadlines, the parent who needs you. Then shape your Ramadan intentions around it. If you miss a day of your new practice, say astaghfirullah and begin again at the next prayer. Returning is part of the practice, and Allah loves those who return to Him.

2026-11-18.title: Your Qur'an companion
2026-11-18.caption:
The Qur'an will speak up for those who kept it company.

The Prophet ﷺ said: read the Qur'an, for it will come on the Day of Resurrection as an intercessor for its companions (Muslim). Companions are people who spend time together, often, and on ordinary days.

When Ramadan arrives, the month of the Qur'an, your reading will flow more easily if the book already feels familiar in your hands.

This week, gather your companion: a mushaf you love, a translation in the language you think in, and one short tafsir or reciter. Then fix a time after one prayer and read a single page with its meaning. Copy one verse into a small notebook each day, with a line about why it stayed with you.

2026-11-19.title: Your du'a list
2026-11-19.caption:
At iftar, your mind may go blank. A list helps.

There are moments in Ramadan we will long to use well: the minutes before iftar, the last third of the night, the hour on Friday. Hearts are full, yet words can disappear.

Allah says: when My servants ask you about Me, I am near (2:186). This verse comes in the middle of the verses about fasting, a gentle sign of where du'a belongs.

Start your list today, in a small notebook or a note on your phone. Organise it in four corners: your deen, your people, your dunya, the ummah. Write names. Add one du'a each day. Then use the list now, in sujood and between the adhan and iqamah, so that by Ramadan the words already feel familiar on your tongue.

2026-11-20.title: Jumu'ah and Surah al-Kahf
2026-11-20.caption:
Today is one of twelve Fridays left before Ramadan.

The Prophet ﷺ called Friday the best day on which the sun rises (Muslim). It is also a beautiful place to practise the habits you hope to carry into Ramadan.

Surah al-Kahf on Friday is a well-loved Sunnah: a light shines for the reader between the two Fridays (al-Hakim, al-Bayhaqi). If one sitting feels long, read it in four parts: after Fajr, at lunch, after Asr and before Maghrib.

Add salawat on the Prophet ﷺ, a number you can keep, and protect the last hour before Maghrib for du'a. Inside al-Kahf you will meet the du'a of the young people of the cave: our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself, and set right for us our affair (18:10).

2026-11-21.title: Sleep before Ramadan
2026-11-21.caption:
Your best morning starts the night before.

In Ramadan, nights will change shape: tarawih, a short sleep, suhoor, Fajr. The body adjusts more kindly when it already has a steady rhythm.

The Prophet ﷺ disliked sleeping before Isha and idle talk after it (Bukhari), and he made du'a for barakah in the early mornings of his ummah (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi). Together they describe a simple evening: pray Isha, wind down, sleep, rise for Fajr.

This week, choose one change. Put the phone in another room after Isha. Make wudu before bed, lie on your right side and recite your adhkar for sleep, as the Prophet ﷺ taught (Bukhari, Muslim). After Fajr, stay up for ten minutes of dhikr or Qur'an before the day pulls at you.

2026-11-22.title: Family and Ramadan
2026-11-22.caption:
What will your children remember about this Ramadan?

Ramadan memories are made at home: the smell of the iftar table, the sound of Qur'an after Maghrib, a parent waking a child gently for suhoor. Preparing as a family begins long before the first fast.

Allah tells us to enjoin prayer on our families and to be patient in it (20:132). Patience is the key word: small, steady invitations, repeated with love.

This Sunday, gather everyone for one calm conversation. Ask each person what they love about Ramadan and what they would like to do differently this year. Then agree on one shared practice to start now: a du'a jar, a page of Qur'an after Maghrib, a sadaqa box by the door, or a countdown calendar the children decorate.

2026-11-23.title: Work and fasting
2026-11-23.caption:
Your Ramadan workday can be rehearsed this week.

Today is a Monday, and also the 13th of Jumada al-Akhirah, the first of the white days. The Prophet ﷺ fasted on Mondays (Muslim) and encouraged fasting the 13th, 14th and 15th of each lunar month (Nasa'i, Tirmidhi).

If you are able, a voluntary fast this week is a gentle rehearsal. Notice when your focus is sharpest, which meetings drain you, and where the afternoon dips. Those notes become your Ramadan work plan: deep work early, lighter tasks before Asr, and kindness to yourself near iftar.

If you are not fasting this week, keep the same intention: plan your workday as if you were, and fill the gaps with dhikr.

Allah says: my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah (6:162). Your work belongs in that sentence too.

2026-11-24.title: Your sadaqa plan
2026-11-24.caption:
One seed, seven ears, a hundred grains in each.

Allah describes sadaqa as a seed that grows seven ears, with a hundred grains in each, and He multiplies it further for whom He wills (2:261).

Ramadan giving flows more easily when it is planned. Take ten minutes this week with four questions: which causes are closest to your heart, how much you can give without strain, how often you will give, and when your zakat is due, if it is.

Then start now. Choose a small amount and set it as a standing order, so it continues on tired days. Let one gift this week be known only to Allah. The Prophet ﷺ told us that sadaqa does not decrease wealth (Muslim).

If money is tight, sadaqa has many doors: a smile, a kind word, a meal cooked for someone, time given to a lonely relative.

2026-11-25.title: The tongue
2026-11-25.caption:
A hungry stomach is the easier part of fasting.

The Prophet ﷺ said: whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, Allah has no need of his giving up food and drink (Bukhari). The fast reaches all the way to the tongue.

This week, notice where your words slip. Maybe it is a comment about someone who is not in the room, a sharp reply when you are tired, or a voice note sent before the anger settles. Noticing is the first step, and it needs no guilt.

Then try a pause. Before you speak, ask: is it true, is it kind, is it needed? If the answer is unclear, say SubhanAllah and wait. Each pause trains the self you will bring into Ramadan.

2026-11-26.title: Screens and the eyes
2026-11-26.caption:
How many times did you reach for your phone today?

Screens take more than time. They take the quiet minutes after salah, the sleep that would carry you through suhoor, and the attention meant for the people beside you.

In the hadith of Jibril, the Prophet ﷺ described ihsan: to worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, He surely sees you (Muslim). Remembering that Allah sees is the gentlest screen boundary there is.

This week, set three boundaries. Unfollow five accounts that leave your heart heavy. Leave your phone in another room for every salah and five minutes after. Switch screens off one hour before sleep. Small steps now will keep your Ramadan nights clearer.

2026-11-27.title: The hour of du'a on Friday
2026-11-27.caption:
Where will you be in the last hour before Maghrib?

The Prophet ﷺ told us there is an hour on Friday in which a believer asks Allah for good and is given it (Bukhari, Muslim). Many scholars look for it in the final hour before Maghrib, based on narrations in Abu Dawud and Nasa'i.

On a busy Friday that hour often fills with cooking, traffic and the school run. This week, protect ten or fifteen minutes of it. Finish errands before Asr, make wudu, face the qibla, and open the du'a list you began last week. Ask for your deen, your people, your dunya and the ummah.

This is a habit to carry into Ramadan, when the same hour comes with the fast.

2026-11-29.title: Lessons from the free class

Why, how, and for whom: three questions for every task.

It comes from Al-Ghazali's Ihya, in his book on vigilance and self-accounting. He calls it mushāraṭa: setting conditions with the self each morning, as a merchant agrees terms with a partner.

In practice, it is three questions before any important task. Why am I doing this? How will I do it well? For whom am I doing it? The answers are your niyyah, and the Prophet ﷺ taught that actions are by intentions (Bukhari, Muslim).

Sha'ban begins on Saturday 9 January. Water your seeds daily, and use these weeks to make up any missed fasts, as Aisha did (Bukhari, Muslim).

Ramadan is expected on Monday 8 February. Carry what you planted into the fast, and make du'a for the harvest. The fruit is from Allah; the planting is ours.

2026-12-06.title: The four sacred months
2026-12-06.caption:
In four days, a sacred month begins, in sha Allah.

During his farewell pilgrimage, the Prophet ﷺ reminded us that the year is twelve months, four of them sacred: Dhul-Qa'dah, Dhul-Hijjah, Muharram, and Rajab, which comes between Jumada and Sha'ban (Bukhari, Muslim).

Rajab is expected to begin on Thursday 10 December. Many scholars teach that in the sacred months good deeds weigh more and wrongs weigh more too, so the believer is careful with both. There are no special prayers to invent; the well-known Sunnah is more than enough.

Use these four days to prepare. Mend one tie you have let drift. Name one habit you want to leave during the sacred month. And choose the single good practice you will plant on 1 Rajab, then ask Allah to accept it.

2026-12-10.title: 1 Rajab: a sacred month begins
2026-12-10.caption:
Today is 1 Rajab. The planting begins.

Allah tells us that the number of months with Him is twelve, four of them sacred, so do not wrong yourselves in them (9:36). Rajab is one of the four, and today, in sha Allah, it begins. Dates here follow the Umm al-Qura calendar, and local moon sighting may differ by a day.

Abu Bakr al-Balkhi, quoted by Ibn Rajab, called Rajab the month of planting, Sha'ban the month of watering, and Ramadan the month of harvest. So today, plant one seed. Name one practice, make it small enough for your hardest day, and ask Allah to make it grow.

Honour the month with care: guard your tongue and your dealings, do more good, and keep to the well-known Sunnah.

2026-12-11.title: Plant one seed this Rajab
2026-12-11.caption:
Two days into Rajab, and the ground is ready for one seed.

Rajab is one of the four sacred months Allah mentions in Surah at-Tawbah (9:36), with a clear instruction: do not wrong yourselves in them. So this month, guard against wrong, and plant one good deed you can keep.

Keep it small enough to survive a busy Tuesday. Two rak'ahs after Isha. One page of Qur'an after Fajr. A small sadaqa set aside before work. Attach it to something you already do, make your niyyah, ask Allah for help, and begin today. Allah sees an atom's weight of good, so no seed is too small to count.

Abu Bakr al-Balkhi, quoted by Ibn Rajab, called Rajab the month of planting, Sha'ban the month of watering, and Ramadan the month of harvest. A seed planted now has eight weeks to take root.

2026-12-12.title: Mushāraṭa: set your terms
2026-12-12.caption:
Before the day sets your terms, set them yourself.

In Book 38 of the Ihya, Al-Ghazali describes six stations of watchfulness over the self. The first is mushāraṭa: setting conditions. He pictures a merchant who hands goods to a partner and agrees the terms in advance. Here the partner is your own self, and the goods are the hours of your life.

He suggests a striking way to begin. After Fajr, imagine that your life had ended and Allah gave you back one single day. How would you spend it?

Try it today in two minutes. Name the day. Choose one thing to guard: your tongue, your eyes or your time. Choose one good deed to do before Maghrib. Then make du'a, and leave the outcome with Allah.

Over the coming weeks we will walk through all six stations, one at a time, so they feel familiar by the time Ramadan arrives.

2026-12-13.title: Istighfar, a daily polish
2026-12-13.caption:
A heart gathers dust the way a window does: quietly, every day.

The Prophet ﷺ described it for us. When a servant sins, a dark spot forms on the heart, and when they stop and seek forgiveness, the heart is polished clean (Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah). And he ﷺ, the best of creation, sought Allah's forgiveness more than seventy times a day.

Istighfar needs very little. It can be said at the sink, on the school run, in the pharmacy queue, on days you pray and on days you don't.

This week, anchor it to three moments. Three times after each salah, as the Prophet ﷺ did after the salam. A count of one hundred on your daily drive or walk. And Sayyid al-Istighfar once before sleep, read slowly from a card by your bed.

By the time Ramadan arrives, these words will already sit easily on your tongue.

2026-12-14.title: Mondays and Thursdays
2026-12-14.caption:
Winter days are short, which makes this the kindest season to practise.

The Prophet ﷺ regularly fasted on Mondays and Thursdays. He explained that deeds are presented to Allah on these two days, and he loved for his deeds to be presented while he was fasting (Tirmidhi). Monday held another meaning for him: the day he was born and the day revelation began (Muslim).

A practice fast now does two things. It follows a beloved Sunnah, and it reminds your body, gently, how a fasting day feels: the early suhoor, the slower afternoon, the first date at Maghrib.

Choose one day this week or next. Prepare suhoor the night before, keep the afternoon light, and plan a simple iftar. If you owe fasts from last Ramadan, this is a good day to make one up.

If you cannot fast this week, mark the day with extra dhikr, a sadaqa, or a meal for someone who is fasting.

2026-12-15.title: Start your Qur'an plan now
2026-12-15.caption:
Four pages after each salah is roughly a full khatm in Ramadan.

Most Qur'an plans fail in the first week of Ramadan because they start in the first week of Ramadan. Beginning now gives your plan eight weeks to settle into your days.

Start with your niyyah: what do you hope to read when Ramadan arrives? Then count backwards. Thirty juz across thirty days comes to about four pages after each of the five prayers. If that feels far away, read one page after Fajr this week and add one page each week. By Sha'ban, the rhythm will already be yours.

If your recitation is slow, take heart. The Prophet ﷺ said that the one who recites with difficulty, stumbling over the words, has a double reward (Bukhari, Muslim). And on days you don't pray, you can still listen, reflect on the meanings, and read tafsir.

2026-12-16.title: Murāqaba: He sees you
2026-12-16.caption:
Someone sees the dishes you wash at midnight.

The second of Al-Ghazali's six stations is murāqaba: the heart's steady awareness that Allah sees it. Yesterday's terms set the direction; murāqaba keeps watch over them through the day.

Its root is the answer the Prophet ﷺ gave Jibril about ihsan: to worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, He surely sees you (Bukhari, Muslim).

Al-Ghazali describes two moments for it. Before an act, you check your intention: for whom am I doing this? During the act, you do it with care, because it is seen. That applies to salah, and also to the email you write, the tone you use with the children, the work you finish when nobody will check it.

Today, set three pause points: before you start a task, once at midday, and once when you are alone. Each time, remind yourself gently: He sees this.

2026-12-17.title: Friday habits for Ramadan
2026-12-17.caption:
Tomorrow is Friday, and tonight is when it gets easier.

The Fridays of Ramadan are precious, and the habits that fill them can be built now. Three Sunnah practices are worth starting this week.

Read Surah al-Kahf on Friday (al-Hakim, Bayhaqi). Send many blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, as he asked us to do on Fridays (Abu Dawud). And seek the hour of answered du'a. The Prophet ﷺ told us there is an hour on Friday in which a believer asking Allah for good is given it (Bukhari, Muslim), and many scholars point to the last hour before Maghrib.

Tonight, make tomorrow simple. Put your mushaf or al-Kahf audio by the bed. Write three du'as on a card. Set a reminder after Asr. Plan an easy dinner so the afternoon stays free for salawat and du'a.

2026-12-18.title: Move your bedtime, gently
2026-12-18.caption:
Your Ramadan nights begin with tonight's bedtime.

When Ramadan arrives, the night changes shape: tarawih after Isha, suhoor before Fajr. If your body already sleeps late and wakes tired, those first days feel heavy. A gentle shift now makes the change far easier.

The Prophet ﷺ disliked sleeping before Isha and talking after it (Bukhari, Muslim). Allah calls sleep a means of rest, a gift. So this week, move lights-out fifteen minutes earlier. Next week, another fifteen. Small enough that your body barely notices.

Help it along. Charge the phone outside the bedroom after Isha. Dim the lights. And close the day with the Sunnah: Ayat al-Kursi and the last three surahs before you sleep (Bukhari).

Jumu'ah mubarak. May Allah put barakah in your rest and in your waking.

2026-12-19.title: Clearing envy, pride and anger
2026-12-19.caption:
A heart needs clearing, the way a home does before guests arrive.

Ramadan will arrive as a guest worth preparing for, and three things crowd the heart more than most: envy, pride and anger. They rarely announce themselves. They show up as a tightness when a sister shares good news, a struggle to say "I was wrong", a sharp reply replayed later in the shower.

The Sunnah gives a response for each. When envy rises, say "ma sha Allah" and ask Allah for barakah in what she has. When pride rises, remember Who gave you the gift and say "alhamdulillah". When anger rises, seek refuge in Allah from Shaytan (Bukhari, Muslim), and if you are standing, sit down (Abu Dawud).

Allah praises those who restrain their anger and pardon people, and He loves those who do good (3:134). Choose one of the three to watch this week, and make du'a for a clean heart.

2026-12-20.title: Muḥāsaba: the evening review
2026-12-20.caption:
Close the day the way a careful merchant closes her books.

The third of Al-Ghazali's six stations is muḥāsaba, self-accounting. Each evening, he says, sit with your self as a merchant sits with a partner and settle the accounts. Your obligations are the capital. Extra good deeds are the profit. Wrongs are the loss, to be repaired.

He reminds us of the words reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: take account of yourselves before you are taken to account. And Allah describes a book that leaves out nothing, small or great (18:49).

Tonight, take five minutes after Isha. Check the capital: did I pray on time, did I meet today's duties? Count the profit: one good deed, and a word of thanks to Allah. Note the loss: one wrong, an istighfar, and a small repair for tomorrow.

Keep the tone honest and kind. The aim is a clearer tomorrow.

2026-12-21.title: The white days begin tomorrow
2026-12-21.caption:
Look up tomorrow night: the moon will be almost full.

The 13th, 14th and 15th of every lunar month are known as the white days, named for the bright moon that lights their nights. The Prophet ﷺ advised Abu Dharr: if you fast any days of the month, fast these three (Nasa'i, Tirmidhi).

This is a Sunnah for every month of the year, and this month it falls on Tuesday 22, Wednesday 23 and Thursday 24 December. Keeping it now is a gentle rehearsal: three short winter fasts, with time to notice how your body and your days respond.

Choose what fits. All three days, or one. Prepare suhoor tonight so the morning is easy. And if you are not fasting this week, mark the days in other ways: extra dhikr, a sadaqa, or a meal for someone who is fasting.

Today is also a Monday, so if you would like an early start, the door is open today too.

2026-12-22.title: Tawbah: the door is open
2026-12-22.caption:
Every night and every day, the door stays open.

Some of us carry a mistake for months, waiting for the right moment to bring it to Allah. The Prophet ﷺ told us that Allah extends His hand at night to accept the repentance of the one who sinned by day, and by day for the one who sinned by night (Muslim). The right moment is today.

Tawbah means returning. Scholars describe its heart as sincere regret, stopping the wrong, and resolving to leave it. When the wrong touched someone else, returning their right is part of the return.

Find a quiet moment, after Isha or before Fajr. Speak to Allah honestly, in your own words and your own language. Then take one concrete step today that moves you away from what you regret.

Today is also the first of the white days, and Rajab is a sacred month. A fitting day to begin again.

Today's journal prompt: What did a hard moment this week teach me about myself?

2026-12-23.title: Mu'āqaba: correct course with kindness
2026-12-23.caption:
You slipped yesterday. What you do next is where growth begins.

The fourth of Al-Ghazali's six stations is mu'āqaba. After the evening review, when you find a lapse, you respond to it on purpose. Al-Ghazali recounts early Muslims who, after a moment of heedlessness, gave something precious in charity, so the self would learn that each slip brings a good deed after it.

The Qur'an reminds us that each of us is a clear witness over our own self, even when we offer excuses (75:14–15). Mu'āqaba takes that honesty and turns it into action.

Keep your repairs kind and firm. Missed a prayer? Pray it as soon as you remember, then add two voluntary rak'ahs. Spoke sharply? Apologise today and give a small sadaqa. Lost an evening to the screen? Give the next fifteen free minutes to Qur'an or dhikr.

Today is the second of the white days, a good day for a fresh start.

2026-12-24.title: Your sadaqa, on autopilot
2026-12-24.caption:
The best sadaqa plan keeps running on your busiest days.

Most of us intend to give more before Ramadan, and then the week fills up. Setting it up once solves that. A small daily donation to a trusted charity, a coin jar by the front door, a family sadaqa box the children add to after Maghrib: each one keeps giving whether or not you remember.

Allah describes charity given in His way as a single seed that grows seven ears, with a hundred grains in each, and He multiplies for whom He wills (2:261). The amount on your screen may look tiny. What Allah does with it is in His hands.

Make your niyyah when you set it up, and renew it whenever you notice it leave your account. On days you are not praying or fasting, your sadaqa keeps flowing, and so can your smile, your kind word, the meal you share.

Today is the last of the white days. A good day to plant this.

2026-12-25.title: Ties of kinship before Ramadan
2026-12-25.caption:
Somewhere, a relative would love to hear your voice this week.

The school holidays bring families closer, on the sofa and on the phone. It is a natural moment to tend the ties that have grown thin: the aunt who hears from you only at Eid, the cousin you drifted from after a misunderstanding, the sibling in another time zone, the elderly relative who would treasure ten minutes of your time.

Islam places great weight on ties of kinship, and in Ramadan they gather around the same iftar table. Repairing them now means arriving at Ramadan with a lighter heart.

Write three names. This weekend, call one, simply to ask how they are. And where someone hurt you, Allah gives a beautiful instruction: repel evil with what is better, and the one you had enmity with may become like a devoted friend (41:34). It may take more than one call. Make du'a, and leave the result to Allah.

Jumu'ah mubarak.

2026-12-26.title: Rest is part of the plan
2026-12-26.caption:
Your body has a right over you. Plan for it.

Many of us push hard in the weeks before Ramadan and arrive already tired. The Sunnah offers a gentler picture. When Salman al-Farisi found his brother Abu Darda fasting every day and praying all night, he told him: your Lord has a right over you, your self has a right over you, and your family has a right over you, so give each its right. The Prophet ﷺ said: Salman has spoken the truth (Bukhari).

Rest, taken with intention, is part of giving your self its right. It is how you stay able to pray, serve and give when Ramadan arrives.

This weekend, put two hours of real rest in your calendar. Make the niyyah that it will strengthen you for worship. Try a short qaylula, the midday nap the Companions often took, especially before the late nights of tarawih begin.

2026-12-27.title: Make up missed fasts now
2026-12-27.caption:
If you owe fasts, the shortest days of the year are here.

Many sisters carry qada from last Ramadan: days missed through menstruation, pregnancy, nursing, illness or travel. Allah made this easy for us. Whoever is ill or travelling fasts an equal number of other days, and Allah intends ease for us (2:184–185).

Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, would make up her missed fasts in Sha'ban (Bukhari, Muslim). Starting now, in Rajab, gives you even more room: time for the days you cannot fast, for a busy week, for a cold that comes and goes. And winter fasts in the Gulf are short and cool.

This week, write down how many days you owe, calmly and honestly. Spread them across your calendar, one or two a week. Ask a sister who also owes fasts to join you, and break the fast together.

Each qada fast completed lightens what you carry into Ramadan.

Today's journal prompt: What could I forgive, trusting Allah to set it right?

Comment QADA if you are starting this week, and let's make du'a for each other.

2026-12-28.title: Your du'a list, part two
2026-12-28.caption:
Look at your du'a list. Some of it has already been answered.

If you started a du'a list earlier in this countdown, today is for revisiting it. If you haven't, today is a good day to begin.

First, mark what Allah has given, and say alhamdulillah for each one, including the answers that came in a different shape. Then add what has arrived since: new worries, new hopes, new names. Include others: your parents, your children, the sick, the ummah. The Prophet ﷺ taught that when you make du'a for a sister in her absence, an angel says: and for you the same (Muslim).

Add du'as from the Qur'an, like Rabbana atina in Surah al-Baqarah. And sincerely ask Allah to let you reach Ramadan in health and faith.

Allah's promise of nearness, "I am near, I answer the call", sits in the middle of the verses on fasting (2:186). Keep your list where you will see it in Ramadan's last third of the night.

2026-12-29.title: The mental load audit
2026-12-29.caption:
Your head holds a list nobody else can see.

The school form. The dentist. The gift for Friday. Who is eating what, who is upset, which bill is due. Many women carry all of it in their heads, all day, and Ramadan adds iftars, guests, suhoor and Eid on top.

Before that arrives, take twenty minutes this evening. Write every task and worry on one page, without sorting. Then go through it and mark each item in one of three ways: do it, share it, or hand it to Allah in du'a.

The second group matters most. Choose one task and ask one person in your home to own it this week, fully, from start to finish. Sharing the load is part of family life, and the Prophet ﷺ himself helped with the work of his household (Bukhari).

And the third group belongs in your du'a. Allah does not burden a soul beyond what it can bear (2:286).

2026-12-30.title: Mujāhada: steady effort
2026-12-30.caption:
The hardest part of most good deeds is starting them.

The fifth of Al-Ghazali's six stations is mujāhada, striving. He observes that the self often drags its feet when it comes to good deeds and leans towards ease. Mujāhada is the patient answer: you push it gently to do a little more, then you hold that level until it feels natural.

Allah makes a promise to those who strive: "As for those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our ways" (29:69). The striving is ours. The guidance is His.

This week, name the one good deed you keep avoiding. Then make it smaller, until it feels possible today: one page of Qur'an, two rak'ahs, five minutes of dhikr. Repeat it every day, including the tired days. That repetition is the striving.

By the time Ramadan arrives, the deed you resisted in Rajab may be the one that carries you.

2026-12-31.title: Close the year with shukr
2026-12-31.caption:
Tonight the calendar closes. Count your blessings before it does.

As the year ends, many of us look back at what went wrong. Tonight, try looking back with shukr. Allah says: "If you are grateful, I will surely give you more" (14:7).

Sit with a notebook after Isha and write ten blessings from this year, from the large to the very small: a healed relationship, a child's laugh, a prayer that felt close, a door that opened. Then look for the hidden ones, the good that came through a hard moment. Say alhamdulillah for each, and if you wish, make a prostration of thanks, as the Prophet ﷺ did when good news reached him (Abu Dawud).

Carry it forward. Thank the people Allah used to help you; the Prophet ﷺ taught that whoever does not thank people has not thanked Allah (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi). Use one blessing in His obedience this week. And keep the list somewhere you will find it again in Sha'ban.

Today's journal prompt: As the calendar year closes, what do I want to leave in it?

Save this post for tonight, and share it with a sister you are grateful for. 🤍

2027-01-01.title: A fast for the tongue
2027-01-01.caption:
A fast you can begin today: the fast of the tongue.

When Ramadan arrives, we guard our mouths from food and drink. The Sunnah asks us to guard them from harmful words too, and that part takes practice. The Prophet ﷺ gave a simple rule: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let them speak good or remain silent (Bukhari, Muslim).

Today, the first day of the new calendar year and a Friday, try a one-day speech fast. Watch the usual moments: venting about a colleague in the family chat, the small comment about someone else's choices, passing on news you have not checked, the sharp word at home when you are tired.

Before you speak, pause and ask: is it true, is it kind, is it needed? Swap one complaint for dhikr or a word of thanks. Tonight, note where you held back, and thank Allah for it.

Jumu'ah mubarak, and may Allah put barakah in your words this year.

Today's journal prompt: Which family tie has loosened, and how could I reconnect?

2027-01-02.title: Phone boundaries before Ramadan
2027-01-02.caption:
Your phone wakes up before you do. Let's change that.

The minutes after Fajr, the quiet after salah, the last hour before sleep: these are some of the most precious times of the day, and they are often the first ones the phone claims. In Ramadan they become even more precious.

Allah describes the successful believers as those humble in their prayer, and immediately after, as those who turn away from idle talk and vain things (23:1–3). Guarding your attention is part of guarding your salah.

Choose three boundaries today and practise them for the rest of Rajab and Sha'ban. Leave the phone in another room during salah and the dhikr after it. Read Qur'an or the morning adhkar before opening any app. And charge the phone outside the bedroom from Isha onwards.

When Ramadan arrives, these boundaries will already be in place, and your nights will be yours.

Today's journal prompt: Where did I take more than I needed this week?

2027-01-03.title: Talk to work about Ramadan
2027-01-03.caption:
The best time to ask for Ramadan flexibility is five weeks early.

For most offices, tomorrow is the first full week of the new year. Ramadan is expected to begin on Monday 8 February, subject to moon sighting, and a calm conversation now gives your manager time to plan around it.

Prepare first. Know the dates. Read your company's Ramadan hours or leave policy. Then bring a proposal: an earlier start, a protected window before iftar, key meetings placed before noon. If you hope to take leave for the last ten nights, ask now, before the calendar fills.

Frame it as a plan that works for both of you: clear deadlines agreed early, before energy dips, and handovers arranged in advance. The Prophet ﷺ said: make things easy and do not make them difficult (Bukhari, Muslim). A request that eases your team's work too is easier to say yes to.

Make du'a before the conversation, prepare well, and leave the outcome with Allah.

2027-01-04.title: Night prayer: two rak'ahs
2027-01-04.caption:
Two rak'ahs, while the house is asleep.

In Ramadan, many of us hope to stand long in prayer at night. That hope grows more easily from a small habit started now. The Prophet ﷺ told us that our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven in the last third of the night and asks: who is calling upon Me, that I may answer? Who is asking, that I may give? (Bukhari, Muslim)

Start with two rak'ahs. If waking at night feels far off, pray them after Isha, before you sleep, and close with witr, as the Prophet ﷺ taught us to make witr the last of our night prayer (Bukhari, Muslim). If you can, set an alarm fifteen minutes before Fajr and pray them in that quiet.

Recite surahs you know well. Take your time in sujud. Bring one du'a from your list.

Kept daily for five weeks, these two rak'ahs will make tarawih feel familiar when Ramadan arrives.

2027-01-05.title: Choose one surah to understand
2027-01-05.caption:
You recite al-Fatiha seventeen times a day. Do you feel it?

In Ramadan we hear a great deal of Qur'an: in tarawih, at home, on the way to work. Understanding even one surah deeply changes how all of it lands. Allah tells us He sent down a blessed Book so that we may reflect on its verses (38:29).

Choose one surah this week and live with it until Ramadan arrives. A surah you already recite in salah works beautifully, because its meaning will meet you several times a day. Al-Fatiha, recited at least seventeen times daily. Al-Mulk, thirty verses often recited at night. Ad-Duha, for a heavy season. Al-Hujurat, for family and community.

Read a few verses each day with a trusted short tafsir, such as Ibn Kathir's. Then write one line in your journal: the verse that spoke to you today, and why.

Five weeks with one surah, and it will feel like a friend in Ramadan.

2027-01-06.title: Mu'ātaba: honest self-talk, with mercy
2027-01-06.caption:
How do you speak to yourself after a hard day?

The sixth of Al-Ghazali's stations is mu'ātaba, honest self-reproach. He describes speaking to your own self directly, as you would to a friend you love and want to see do better: reminding it of death, of Allah's gaze, of the hours it lets slip away. Allah swears by an-nafs al-lawwama, the self-reproaching soul (75:2), and the scholars describe it as the soul that blames itself and turns back.

This reproach has a direction. It moves you towards change and towards Allah, and it always ends in hope. Allah says: "O My servants who have wronged themselves, do not despair of Allah's mercy" (39:53).

Tonight, try a short, honest conversation with yourself. Name what you did, plainly, with no excuses and no exaggeration. Remind yourself that Allah sees, and that He forgives those who return. Then choose one action for tomorrow and ask Him for help with it.

2027-01-07.title: Rajab review: what took root?
2027-01-07.caption:
Before Rajab closes, take a slow walk through your garden.

At the start of the month we planted one seed: a small, steady deed to carry towards Ramadan. Abu Bakr al-Balkhi, quoted by Ibn Rajab, called Rajab the month of planting and Sha'ban the month of watering. In a day or two, depending on the moon, Sha'ban begins.

So tonight, sit with three questions. What grew? Name the deed you kept, even if only on some days, and thank Allah for it. What struggled? Note what slipped and what made it hard: the time, the place, the tiredness. What will you water? Choose one deed to carry into Sha'ban and strengthen a little.

If very little took root, there is room to begin again. Sha'ban offers about four more weeks. Start with the smallest version of your deed. Allah says: "My mercy encompasses all things" (7:156).

2027-01-08.title: The six M's, together
2027-01-08.caption:
Six words from Al-Ghazali, one rhythm for Sha'ban.

Over the past weeks we have walked through the six stations Al-Ghazali describes in Book 38 of the Ihya. Today, they come together as one simple daily system.

In the morning, after Fajr: mushāraṭa. Set your terms, one thing to guard and one good deed to give. Through the day: murāqaba. At each prayer, pause and remember that He sees you, and check your niyyah. In the evening: muḥāsaba, a five-minute review. Then mu'āqaba, one kind repair for a lapse. Mujāhada, a small push on the deed you resist. And mu'ātaba, an honest word with yourself that ends in hope.

Keep it small. The Prophet ﷺ said the most beloved deeds to Allah are those done consistently, even if they are small (Bukhari, Muslim).

2027-01-09.title: 1 Sha'ban: the month of watering
2027-01-09.caption:
Sha'ban has begun. The seeds of Rajab are ready for water.

Abu Bakr al-Balkhi, quoted by Ibn Rajab, called Sha'ban the month of watering. It was a month the Prophet ﷺ prepared in. Aisha said she never saw him fast more in any month than in Sha'ban (Bukhari, Muslim), and she would make up her own missed Ramadan fasts in it.

This week, water what you planted. Add one fast, voluntary or qada. Add a little to the deed you began in Rajab: one more page, two more rak'ahs, a slightly larger sadaqa. And if you can, find sisters to prepare with, so the weeks ahead stay steady.

2027-01-10.title: Why the Prophet ﷺ fasted Sha'ban
2027-01-10.caption:
He fasted more in Sha'ban than in any other month.

Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, described it plainly: outside Ramadan, she never saw the Prophet ﷺ fast more in any month than in Sha'ban. When he was asked about it, he spoke of a month people neglect, between Rajab and Ramadan, when deeds are raised to Allah.

So Sha'ban carries two gifts for you. It is a month of following his sunnah, and it is a month of practice. A few fasts now teach your body the rhythm of suhoor and iftar, so the first days of Ramadan feel familiar.

Start with what you owe. If you have qada from last Ramadan, those fasts come first; Aisha herself would make hers up in Sha'ban. Then add a Monday or Thursday where you can, with a sincere intention and a simple suhoor.

2027-01-11.title: Your Sha'ban rhythm, week by week
2027-01-11.caption:
Sha'ban moves quickly. A simple weekly plan keeps it from slipping past.

Think of the month in four parts. In the first week, settle your fasts: qada first, then a Monday or Thursday if you can. In the second and third weeks, build the daily practices you want in Ramadan: a few more pages of Qur'an, earlier nights, a real suhoor, iftars that are easy to cook.

The last week belongs to the heart. Seek forgiveness from Allah and from people, write your intentions, rest, and prepare your home.

Then give the plan company. The Prophet ﷺ said that a person follows the way of their close friend. Tell one sister your focus for this week and ask hers. A short message each Sunday is enough to keep you both moving.

2027-01-12.title: Qur'an: increase gently
2027-01-12.caption:
Your Ramadan Qur'an is built now, one page at a time.

Many of us plan to read the whole Qur'an in Ramadan from a standing start. Sha'ban gives you four weeks to build up instead.

Begin with an honest number: how much do you read on an ordinary day today? Keep that amount, then add one page each Sunday. Tie your reading to a prayer you already pray, so it has a fixed home in the day. Leave your mushaf open where you will see it.

On the days you are tired, read one verse slowly and reflect on it. Allah tells us four times in Surah al-Qamar that He has made the Qur'an easy to remember. Trust that ease, and keep showing up.

2027-01-13.title: Rehearse your Ramadan sleep
2027-01-13.caption:
The hardest part of the first Ramadan week is often the sleep.

In Ramadan, iftar and tarawih push the evening later, and suhoor calls you up before Fajr. When the change arrives all at once, the first days can feel heavy.

Sha'ban is your rehearsal. Move your bedtime earlier in small steps, fifteen minutes every few nights. Twice a week, set an alarm before Fajr and pray two rak'ahs of tahajjud, even short ones. If your day allows, take a short rest after Dhuhr, a sunnah the Companions knew as qaylula.

Allah describes rising at night as firmer in its effect and more suited for recitation. Those quiet minutes before Fajr can become the part of Ramadan you look forward to most.

If you are a mother with small children, your nights may already be broken. Count those wakings as a chance for a short du'a, and rest when you can.

2027-01-14.title: Suhoor and water, practised now
2027-01-14.caption:
Many tired afternoons in Ramadan begin with a rushed suhoor.

The Prophet ﷺ told us there is blessing in suhoor, and he encouraged it even if it is only a sip of water. Sha'ban, with its sunnah fasts, is the perfect place to learn what works for your body.

On your next fast, prepare suhoor the night before: oats or eggs, bread, yoghurt, a few dates, and a full jug of water by the kitchen sink. Between iftar and suhoor, spread your water out: two glasses at iftar, two during the evening, two at suhoor. Keep salty food and strong coffee light, since both leave you thirsty.

Then pay attention. At Asr, write two lines: what you ate, and how you feel. After three or four fasts, you will know your own suhoor.

2027-01-15.title: Friday: the hour of du'a, again
2027-01-15.caption:
Before Maghrib today, give yourself the most hopeful hour of the week.

The Prophet ﷺ told us of an hour on Friday when Allah gives a believer the good they ask for. Many scholars hoped for it in the final hour before Maghrib, so that is a good place to start.

This morning, write three du'as on a small card. One for your Ramadan: the worship you hope for, the habit you want to leave behind. One for your family. One for the ummah. In the afternoon, set the phone in another room, pause the kitchen, and sit with your card. Raise your hands and ask with certainty.

If something has been holding you back from a good you want to do, name it in that hour too. Say, as the believers said, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs."

2027-01-16.title: Simple iftars and a freezer plan
2027-01-16.caption:
A full freezer in Sha'ban means calmer evenings in Ramadan.

The hour before Maghrib is precious: it is a time for du'a, and often the time we spend standing at the stove. A little cooking now can give some of that hour back.

This weekend, write a simple seven-day iftar rota from meals your family already loves. Pick two dishes that freeze well, such as a lentil soup and a tray of marinated chicken, and cook double. Freeze half in labelled portions. Repeat each weekend, and by the end of Sha'ban you will have a small stock ready.

Keep iftar itself simple: dates, water, soup, one main dish. The Prophet ﷺ told us that whoever gives iftar to a fasting person receives a reward like theirs. Each portion you freeze can carry that intention.

2027-01-17.title: Your Ramadan budget
2027-01-17.caption:
Ramadan spending can drift. A short plan written today keeps it gentle.

Allah describes His servants as those who spend without waste and without stinginess, keeping a just balance. A Ramadan budget is simply a way to live that verse.

Open your banking app and look at last Ramadan: groceries, takeaways, Eid shopping, giving. Then set four envelopes for this year. Food, including the guests you hope to host. Sadaqa, as a daily amount, so you give every single day. Eid, including zakat al-fitr for each person in your household. And zakat al-mal, if yours falls due and you choose to pay it in Ramadan.

If your platform allows it, schedule a small daily donation now for all thirty days. Then the giving happens even on the tiring days.

2027-01-18.title: Children and Ramadan
2027-01-18.caption:
Children often remember Ramadan by how the house felt.

The smell of iftar, the jar of dates on the table, a parent reading Qur'an after Fajr. The traditions you start in Sha'ban become their memories of Ramadan.

Match each child to what they can do. Little ones can count down the days and drop the sadaqa coin. Primary-age children can practise a half-day fast on a weekend, if they want to. Pre-teens can learn a short surah to pray beside you. Teenagers can plan an iftar or a small charity project themselves.

This week, try three things. Start a countdown jar with one good-deed note a day. Read one story of a Prophet at bedtime. Give each child a job at iftar.

Allah tells us to enjoin prayer on our families and to be steadfast in it ourselves. Your own calm worship teaches them more than any lecture.

2027-01-19.title: Build your day around salah
2027-01-19.caption:
Your Ramadan planner already exists. It is the five prayer times.

Instead of fitting salah around a busy day, try building the day around salah. Each prayer opens a new block, and each block can hold one kind of work.

Fajr to Dhuhr is usually your clearest stretch: Qur'an first, then your most focused tasks. Dhuhr to Asr suits meetings, errands and a short rest. Asr to Maghrib is for light cooking and the precious minutes of du'a before iftar. After Maghrib come iftar, Isha and tarawih.

Rehearse it this week. At the top of each day, write the five prayer times. Place your hardest task in the block after Fajr. Protect fifteen minutes before Maghrib. When you work inside these blocks, you do each task with more care, and the prayers stay at the centre.

2027-01-20.title: The white days begin tomorrow
2027-01-20.caption:
Tomorrow, the white days of Sha'ban begin.

The Prophet ﷺ advised fasting the 13th, 14th and 15th of each lunar month, the days when the moon is full and bright. This month they fall on Thursday 21, Friday 22 and Saturday 23 January, according to the expected calendar.

In Sha'ban, these days carry extra meaning. They follow his sunnah of fasting much of this month, and they give your body three days of practice before thirty. If you still owe qada from last Ramadan, you can make those fasts up on these days instead.

Tonight, make your intention: a sunnah fast or a qada fast. Set out your suhoor before bed. Look at Thursday and move one heavy task, so the day feels lighter.

If you can only fast one or two of the three, do what you can with sincerity. Allah sees the effort.

2027-01-21.title: Reduce before you add
2027-01-21.caption:
A cup that is already full cannot take in more.

We often prepare for Ramadan by adding: more Qur'an, more prayer, more giving. Those are beautiful intentions. They also need space, and most of our days are already full.

So begin by clearing. Notice where your hours slip away: scrolling in bed, group chats through the evening, shows waiting in a watch list, commitments you agreed to without thinking.

This week, choose three small changes. Move your most-used app off the home screen until Eid. Mute busy group chats and check them once a day. Step back, politely, from one optional commitment during Ramadan.

In Surah al-Mu'minun, Allah describes the successful believers as those who turn away from idle talk. Each time you set one aside, you make room for dhikr, for rest, and for the people you love.

Today is also the first white day. If you are fasting, may Allah accept it.

2027-01-22.title: Friday: clear your heart
2027-01-22.caption:
Some of what we carry is invisible: an old hurt, a resentment.

The Prophet ﷺ told us that on the night of mid-Sha'ban, Allah looks at His creation and forgives everyone except one who associates partners with Him and one who holds a grudge. According to the expected calendar, that night begins at Maghrib this evening. There is no special ritual for it. It is a reminder to let go.

Today is also Jumu'ah, with its hour of answered du'a. Use it. Write the name of one person you find hard to forgive. In the afternoon, ask Allah to send them good, and to soften your heart toward them. Then recite the du'a of Surah al-Hashr: "Our Lord, leave no resentment in our hearts toward those who believe."

Then turn to gratitude. Write three ways Allah has helped you grow since last Ramadan. A grateful heart lets go more easily.

2027-01-23.title: Mid-Sha'ban: a heart free of grudges
2027-01-23.caption:
Half of Sha'ban behind you, and a question for your heart.

The Prophet ﷺ told us that Allah looks at His creation on the night of mid-Sha'ban and forgives them all, except one who associates partners with Him and one who holds a grudge. The hadith asks for no special ritual. It carries a clear message: resentment keeps us from forgiveness.

A grudge can be subtle. It shows up when you replay an old conversation, when you feel a small tightness at someone's name, when you avoid a gathering because they will be there.

This weekend, sit with it. Tell Allah honestly how you were hurt. Then make the intention to pardon, even if the feeling takes longer to follow. Finally, make du'a for that person, or send a short, kind message if it is safe and wise to do so.

Forgiving can sit alongside healthy distance from someone who harms you. You are setting the weight down before Allah.

Today's journal prompt: What would I tell my soul today, with honesty and mercy?

2027-01-24.title: Worship on your non-fasting days
2027-01-24.caption:
Some days of Ramadan, you won't fast. You're still inside it.

Many sisters feel left out for a few days each month.

When a woman is on her period or recovering after birth, she does not fast or pray, by Allah's mercy. Yet so much worship remains open: dhikr, du'a, listening to Qur'an, learning tafsir, giving sadaqa, preparing iftar for others. Allah promises forgiveness and a great reward to the women who remember Him often.

Plan those days now, so they feel purposeful. Choose one surah whose tafsir you will study. Write a du'a list for the evenings. Keep a dhikr counter in your bag. Offer to cook iftar for a neighbour or a sister who is busy.

And keep a simple note of the fasts you miss, so you can make them up after Ramadan, with ease, before the next Sha'ban ends.

Today's journal prompt: Which habit would I love to leave behind before Ramadan?

2027-01-25.title: Plan the last ten nights now
2027-01-25.caption:
Your last ten nights of Ramadan are decided in Sha'ban.

By the time Ramadan arrives, the diary fills: work deadlines, school events, Eid preparations. If the last ten nights are not protected now, they get squeezed.

So arrange three things today. Request leave or lighter hours for those dates, if your work allows. Agree with your family who will cook and who will settle the children on those nights. Move social plans and deadlines away from them.

Then sketch a simple plan for each night: two rak'ahs of qiyam, longer on the odd nights; a few pages of Qur'an with meaning; your du'a list, including the du'a the Prophet ﷺ taught Aisha: "O Allah, You are Pardoning and love to pardon, so pardon me." Schedule a small sadaqa for every one of the ten nights, so your giving reaches Laylat al-Qadr, whichever night it is.

Allah tells us this night is better than a thousand months.

2027-01-26.title: I'tikaf: what is possible for you
2027-01-26.caption:
Imagine ten days with Allah as your only appointment.

That is the heart of i'tikaf: staying in the masjid with the intention of worship, set apart from daily affairs. The Prophet ﷺ observed it in the last ten days of Ramadan every year, and after him his wives continued it.

For many sisters, especially mothers and those who work, a full ten days may not be possible. Plan for what is. Contact your local masjid this week and ask whether it hosts women for i'tikaf, and how. If you can go, plan which days or nights you will give.

If you cannot, you can still create a nightly retreat at home. It is not i'tikaf in the technical sense, yet it carries the same longing: a prayer corner, the phone in another room, a Qur'an, your du'a list, and a few protected hours each night.

Make du'a now that Allah grants you the closest form available to you.

Today's journal prompt: What is my heart's deepest du'a right now?

2027-01-27.title: Prepare Eid early
2027-01-27.caption:
The busiest malls of the year open during the last ten nights.

Many of us end Ramadan in shopping queues, searching for shoes the night before Eid. Those hours could be spent in qiyam and du'a instead.

So bring Eid forward. This week, make one focused trip or online order for everyone's clothes, and try them on at home. Buy and wrap gifts for the children in your family, and store them away. Write down the zakat al-fitr amount for each person in your household and where you will pay it, so it reaches those in need before the Eid prayer.

Then sketch Eid morning itself: where you will pray, what you will eat, which family you will visit first.

Allah tells us in Surah al-Baqarah that He wants ease for us, that we complete the days of fasting and glorify Him for guiding us. A prepared Eid lets you finish Ramadan with that gratitude.

Today's journal prompt: What do I hope Allah will find in my heart when Ramadan arrives?

2027-01-28.title: The pantry and shopping list
2027-01-28.caption:
One well-planned shop now can save you a dozen trips in Ramadan.

Supermarkets fill in the hour before iftar. A stocked pantry means you only need quick trips for fresh food, and your afternoons stay calmer.

This weekend, check your cupboards first. Use up what is old and note what is missing. Then write one list, matched to your iftar rota and freezer plan: dates, oats, lentils, rice, tinned tomatoes, chickpeas, spices, frozen vegetables, pastry, water, milk and tea.

Allah tells us to eat and drink without excess. A clear list helps: you buy what you will use, and waste stays low.

Then add one extra bag for someone else: a family you know, or your local food bank. As you pack it, make du'a for them by name, or for those you don't know. The Prophet ﷺ told us that when we pray for a brother or sister in their absence, an angel says, "And for you the same."

2027-01-29.title: Friday: ask to reach Ramadan
2027-01-29.caption:
Every Ramadan, someone who was planning for it does not reach it.

That thought is sobering, and it is also a gift. It reminds us that Allah alone decides who reaches Ramadan, and that every day of fasting is His mercy.

This Friday, during the hour before Maghrib, make three du'as in your own words. Ask Allah to let you reach Ramadan in health and faith. Ask Him to accept your fasting, your prayer and your giving. Ask Him to forgive what came before, so you begin lighter. Scholars of the early generations would ask Allah, for months, to let them reach Ramadan. You can join that longing today.

If you carry regret from last year, or a habit you are ashamed of, take comfort in Surah az-Zumar. Allah calls those who have wronged themselves "My servants", and tells them never to despair of His mercy.

Today's journal prompt: What do I need to forgive myself for?

2027-01-30.title: A lighter home before Ramadan
2027-01-30.caption:
Your home will host thirty suhoors and thirty iftars.

Give it a little attention this weekend. Start with three spaces. First, a prayer corner: clear it, lay the mat, place a Qur'an and a tasbih within reach. Second, the kitchen: empty one cupboard, wipe the counters, and keep only daily tools out, so iftar preparation feels easy. Third, the bedroom: clear the surfaces and put your suhoor alarm by the bed.

As you go, set aside what your family no longer uses: clothes unworn since last Eid, duplicate kitchen tools, toys your children have outgrown. Give the good items as sadaqa before Ramadan begins.

Allah tells us that if we are grateful, He will give us more. Clearing a home is a chance to see how much we have been given. Hold each item for a moment, say alhamdulillah, and pass it on.

Today's journal prompt: What am I most grateful to Allah for this year?

2027-01-31.title: Your digital plan for Ramadan
2027-01-31.caption:
Your phone will either guard your Ramadan or quietly scatter it.

Eight days remain to decide how you will use it. Ten minutes of setup today can carry you through the whole month.

Start with settings. Put a daily limit on social media apps for the thirty days. Move a Qur'an app and a tafsir app onto your home screen. Turn on prayer-time alerts, and add one reminder fifteen minutes before Maghrib for du'a. Schedule focus mode from Isha until after Fajr.

Then set three simple rules. Choose one daily window for social apps. Pick one series of tafsir lessons to follow each night, so you understand what you hear in tarawih. Let people know you may reply more slowly this month.

Allah describes the Qur'an as a blessed Book sent down for reflection. A thoughtful phone can serve that purpose.

Today's journal prompt: Which part of the Qur'an do I hope to understand better this Ramadan?

2027-02-01.title: One week: the final checklist
2027-02-01.caption:
One week from today, Ramadan is expected to begin.

Today, sit down with a cup of tea and one page. Walk through the essentials. Have you made up your qada fasts, or planned the last ones for this week? Are the freezer, pantry and iftar rota ready? Have you requested leave for the last ten nights? Are Eid clothes, gifts and zakat al-fitr sorted?

Tick what is done. For what remains, decide quickly: do it this week, hand it to someone, or drop it. A plan that is ninety per cent ready is enough.

Then say no once. Choose one invitation, project or task that would crowd the first week, and decline it kindly.

Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ in Surah ash-Sharh: when you have finished, stand in worship, and turn your longing to your Lord. Finish the practical tasks, then turn toward Him.

Today's journal prompt: What will I say no to, so I can say yes to Ramadan?

2027-02-02.title: Write your Ramadan intentions
2027-02-02.caption:
Your most important Ramadan page fits on an index card.

The Prophet ﷺ said that actions are only by intentions, and each person will have what they intended. A sincere intention is already rewarded, even before the deed.

Today, write your Ramadan intentions by hand, in three layers. With Allah: your fasting, prayer, Qur'an, and the du'as you will make. With people: your family, the sisters you'll support, the people you'll feed. With yourself: one habit to leave behind and one to grow.

Begin each line with "In shaa Allah, I intend to...". Keep the card inside your mushaf or on your prayer mat, and read it each night after tarawih.

Then renew small intentions for ordinary things: cooking iftar to nourish the fasting, working to provide, sleeping to rise for suhoor. Make du'a, do your part, and leave the outcome with Allah.

Today's journal prompt: How do I hope to feel on the night of Eid?

2027-02-03.title: Seek people's forgiveness
2027-02-03.caption:
There may be one message you've been meaning to send for months.

The Prophet ﷺ told us that whoever has wronged someone, in their honour or anything else, should seek their pardon today, before a day when there is no money to settle accounts, only good and bad deeds.

Think of the people you may owe: a parent or sibling you spoke harshly to, a friend you let down, a colleague you criticised unfairly, someone you owe money. Choose one and reach out this week.

Keep it short and sincere: "I'm sorry for what I said. Please forgive me." You do not need to explain everything. Repay debts, or agree a plan for them. Then send a warm message to your wider family, asking them to forgive any hurt before Ramadan.

You cannot control how people respond. Your part is to ask with humility, and Allah sees your effort.

Returning to Allah begins with the heart, and often passes through the people around us.

Today's journal prompt: What does returning to Allah mean to me today?

2027-02-04.title: Your Ramadan rhythm on one page
2027-02-04.caption:
Four days left. Gather everything onto a single sheet.

Over Sha'ban you have planned a lot: Qur'an pages, sleep, suhoor, iftars, budget, the last ten nights, Eid. Now bring it together so you can follow it at a glance.

In the centre, write the times: the five prayers, suhoor, iftar and tarawih. In the corners, your daily acts: Qur'an pages, dhikr, your sadaqa amount, one kind deed. At the bottom, one focus for each ten nights of Ramadan, and your Eid plan. At the top, write one verse you want to reflect on all month.

Choose daily acts small enough to keep on your hardest day. The Prophet ﷺ told us that the deeds most beloved to Allah are the consistent ones, even if small. Add a box for each day to tick, and be gentle on the days you miss.

Put one copy on the fridge and one in your bag.

2027-02-05.title: A letter for the last night
2027-02-05.caption:
Write a letter today for the last night of Ramadan.

On that night, you will likely be tired, hopeful, perhaps a little sad that the month is ending. A letter from today's you can meet you there with a reminder of what you hoped for.

Keep it short. Five lines are enough. What you hope Allah will change in you this month. The du'a you most want answered. A word of mercy for the days you might fall short. One habit you hope to carry past Eid. Close with a du'a for your future self.

Seal it in an envelope, write "Open on the last night" on the front, and tuck it inside your mushaf or journal.

Allah tells us to look to what we send ahead for tomorrow. This letter is a small way of doing that: sending hope forward, and preparing to meet yourself with kindness.

It is also Jumu'ah. Add your letter's du'a to your Friday asking this afternoon.

2027-02-06.title: Rest, and prepare your heart
2027-02-06.caption:
Two days before Ramadan, the best preparation may be rest.

You've spent Sha'ban planning, cooking, clearing, forgiving and writing. Whatever is still unfinished can wait, or be left with Allah. Today, give your body and heart a quiet day.

Sleep a little longer, or nap after Dhuhr. Eat simply and drink plenty of water. Read the fasting verses of Surah al-Baqarah, 183 to 187, slowly, with a translation. Sit outside for a few minutes of dhikr.

This evening, say istighfar slowly before you sleep. Read your intentions card again, and ask Allah to accept it. Find out when and how your local community will announce the moon sighting, so you are ready either way.

Allah tells us why we fast in one line: so that we may become mindful of Him. Let that be the intention you carry into the month.

Today's journal prompt: Ramadan is almost here. What is my intention for this blessed month?

2027-02-07.title: Tomorrow, in shaa Allah
2027-02-07.caption:
Ramadan is expected to begin tomorrow, in shaa Allah.

According to the Umm al-Qura calendar, the first fast is expected on Monday 8 February, subject to moon sighting. Follow your local announcement this evening, and stay calm whichever day it falls.

Tonight, keep things simple. Lay out your suhoor: dates, water, something slow. Set your alarm. Make your intention to fast tomorrow once the start is confirmed.

Then sit with Allah for a few minutes. In the middle of the fasting verses, He says: "When My servants ask you about Me, I am near. I respond to the call of the one who calls upon Me." Tell Him what you hope for. Ask Him to accept your fasting and prayer, and to bring you to the end of the month forgiven.

You prepared, in ways big and small. Arrive with gratitude and trust.
